name: lazy-collection
intent: Represent a sequence as a collection-like value whose elements are computed on demand, so an infinite or larger-than-memory sequence can be processed lazily - element work happens only when a consumer asks for it and stops when the consumer stops.
problem: A sequence is unbounded, larger than memory, or expensive per element: materialising it up front (list, array, result set) either fails outright or pays for elements nobody will read, while exposing the production loop to each consumer (or hand-writing a cursor, cache and transformation logic in every call site) duplicates the same bookkeeping and leaks the producer's state. The decision is whether to expose a lazy, collection-shaped abstraction at all, and whether repeated access should recompute elements or memoize them.
context: Applies to in-process sequence abstractions over sources that are produced or fetched rather than already resident - generated or infinite series, files and logs, pages of a remote API, wide query results, large trees and streams - where consumers may stop early or pull one element at a time, where transformations should compose without intermediate collections, and where the language or ecosystem offers a lazy sequence form (generators, iterator adapters, lazy views or collections, deferred query operators). It does not transfer across a process or network boundary: laziness there is pagination or backpressure, not a lazy collection.
benefits: Sequences larger than memory, or unbounded, become processable: memory tracks the working element (plus whatever the memoization policy deliberately retains) instead of the whole sequence.
Work is proportional to demand: elements the consumer never asks for are never computed, fetched or allocated, and an early exit stops production at that point.
Composition keeps the declarative shape while costing a single pass: map/filter/take chains stay lazy and do not build intermediate collections.
Production policy and consumption policy decouple: one source plugs into any consumer or adapter vocabulary, and the consumer decides when to force.
Latency to the first element drops: streaming responses, first-match searches and paged reads hand results back before the source has been traversed.
Optional memoization makes repeated access cheap where recomputation is expensive (lazy list or cached sequence), without forcing eager materialisation up front.
tradeoffs: Evaluation timing becomes implicit: side effects, I/O and exceptions happen at the consumer's pull, far from the code that created the sequence, which moves where failures surface and makes profiling and debugging harder.

Traversal semantics surprise: many realizations are single-use or re-evaluating (Java Stream and JS generators throw or yield nothing on a second pass; IEnumerable, Sequence and lazy views silently recompute), while memoizing realizations retain memory instead.

Retention and space leaks: a memoizing lazy list holds its head and therefore the whole realized prefix, and adapter chains retain their captured sources, closures and buffers for as long as the sequence lives.

Per-element overhead can beat the savings: closure dispatch, boxing and indirection make a lazy chain slower than an index loop for small or hot data - an effect the Kotlin documentation explicitly warns about for sequences.
Algorithms that need all elements (sort, reverse, group-by, count) force materialization and hang on unbounded sources, so laziness must be bounded before it meets them.
Abandoned sequences leak resources: generators, streams and channel-based producers keep frames, file handles or goroutines alive unless they are closed or cancelled deterministically.

participants.responsibility: The collection-shaped value the client holds: knows how to produce element N+1 on demand, keeps the production state private and exposes the traversal contract (single-use or re-iterable, memoized or recomputing).
The thunk, generator frame or source read that produces one element when it is demanded, and only then - it is the unit of work that laziness defers.
Optional: stores elements that have already been forced so repeat access does not recompute them; owns the retention policy and is therefore the source of the classic space leak.

A lazy transformation (map/filter/take/zip/flatMap) attached between source and consumer: it wraps a sequence, applies per element on the way through, and never materializes an intermediate collection.
Drives forcing, decides how many elements to take and when to stop, and owns resource release; it is the only participant that can turn laziness into actual work.
The underlying data producer - an in-memory structure, file, query result, API pages, or an unbounded generative rule - which the lazy sequence reads or wraps.

use_cases: Streaming files, logs and sockets where the input does not fit memory: hand out one line/record/chunk per pull, so a consumer that stops early also stops the reads.
Unbounded or generated series (counters, IDs, timestamps, simulation steps, sensor ticks, property-test inputs) consumed with take/limit/prefix.
Walking paginated remote APIs lazily: fetch page N+1 only when the consumer passes the current page, so a first-match search stops after the page that contains it.
Wide database or ORM result sets and derived projections: iterate rows or computed views without materializing the whole result set.
Composition-heavy transformation over big data: map/filter/flatMap chains that must not build intermediate collections (pairs with deforestation and transducers).
Expensive derived views over existing structures - filtered indices, projected tree walks, sparse-matrix rows - where only part of the result is ever needed.
Real-time log processing pipelines: tail -f style streaming of log lines through filter/map/alert chains where early-match exits prevent full file reads.
ETL and data pipeline ingestion: lazily consume CSV rows, JSON newline-delimited records, or database cursors where downstream transforms may short-circuit on data-quality signals.
Event-sourcing replay: lazily iterate an event store where replay may stop at a snapshot or checkpoint without reading the full history.
Graph traversal frontiers: BFS/DFS lazy frontier queues that never materialize all reachable nodes simultaneously, stopping when a target is found.
Java Stream API pipelines: compose filter/map stages over large or unbounded sources and let short-circuiting terminals consume only the demanded prefix.
C# LINQ IEnumerable queries: defer Where/Select projections until enumeration so a consumer can stop early without materializing the source.
Rust std::iter adapters and Python itertools: build memory-efficient map/filter/take chains over generated or file-backed records, then force them with a consuming operation.
avoid_when: The collection is small and fully consumed: an eager list/array and a plain loop are simpler, faster and easier to test.
Consumers need random access, multiple independent passes or a stable snapshot: materialize deliberately (array/list) or use a persistent data structure.
Elements carry side effects whose order or completeness matters: an eager loop with an explicit sequence of operations does not hide evaluation timing.
The data crosses a process or service boundary: page or stream explicitly with backpressure instead of shipping a lazy handle whose laziness does not survive the wire.
The needed operations require all elements (sort, reverse, group-by, count, join): materialize at a chosen point or use a genuinely streaming algorithm; laziness cannot make those incremental.
anti_patterns: Laziness as a substitute for validation or cleanup: elements reach the consumer before the checks an eager pass would have performed, and early exit skips whatever cleanup that pass owned.
Treating a lazy collection as a re-iterable, thread-safe value: Java streams, JS generators and Go iterators are single-use, so a second traversal throws or silently yields nothing.
Forcing adapter chains over small data where a loop is faster, paying closure/boxing overhead for no memory benefit.
Memoizing every forced element of a huge or unbounded source while holding the head, turning laziness into a space leak.
Running a materializing operation (sorted, count, toList, spread) on an infinite source - a hang written as one line.
Hiding an unbounded lazy sequence behind an API whose other callers iterate it twice, silently duplicating work or losing elements.
Returning a lazy collection from a library API without documenting its traversal contract, leaving consumers unable to predict reuse behavior.
Using a single-use lazy sequence as a cache: repeating the traversal recomputes every element, defeating the purpose for expensive sources.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: the sequence describes what the elements are; the consumer decides when they are computed.
Lazy evaluation as economic design: compute only what is demanded, so cost tracks the benefit actually taken (call-by-need).
Uniformity and composability: finite, infinite, generated and derived sequences share one protocol, so adapters compose without special cases.
Single responsibility: sources produce, adapters transform, terminals force, consumers own the exit policy and the memoization decision.
Information hiding: producer state, buffers and the caching policy stay behind the collection interface.
Explicit over implicit: the traversal contract (single-use vs re-iterable, memoized vs recomputing) must be documented; implicit contracts cause subtle bugs.
best_practices: State the traversal contract explicitly: single-use or re-iterable, memoized or recomputing, thread-safe or not; prefer factories that return a fresh sequence per traversal.
Make cardinality visible: name unbounded sources, bound them at the consumer with take/limit/islice/prefix, and document which operations force everything.
Keep lazy stages pure; move side effects and validation to explicit boundaries so laziness cannot reorder or skip them.
Force deliberately at the orchestration layer: terminal operations belong where the result is needed, not inside adapters or shared helpers.
Release resources deterministically (close/aclose, using/Dispose, with or try/finally, defer plus context) instead of relying on garbage collection for abandoned sequences.
Memoize only when recomputation is expensive and retention is bounded; otherwise prefer recomputation or an explicit materialization point.
Measure before going lazy: for small or hot data an eager loop usually wins.
Profile memory with bounded retention: in memoizing realizations, track the realized prefix size and consider bounded LRU eviction or weak references for long-lived sequences over large data.

Handle exceptions at forcing boundaries: a lazy sequence that raises on the 1000th element surfaces the failure far from its creation site; wrap terminal operations with error context that includes the element index.
Validate inputs at sequence creation, not at forcing time: contract violations caught early are easier to debug than failures that surface mid-traversal.

Prefer language-native lazy forms over hand-rolled implementations: itertools in Python, Java Streams, LINQ in C#, Seq in F#, Rust iterators, and LazyList in Scala are optimized and well-tested; reinventing them risks subtle semantic differences.

Use lazy collections in API boundaries with caution: callers may not expect a sequence to be consumed on a different thread or at an unexpected time; prefer concrete return types where laziness would be surprising.
